claim: CUDA++ is the GPU half of the Omega runtime, under the MIT licence so anyone can use it.
tagline: Bringing CUDA performance to other hardware.
claim_rest: You write a program, CUDA++ runs it. Where a GPU is qualified, it writes that GPU's own machine code, with no vendor user-space stack: no CUDA toolkit, no nvcc, no PTX, no libcuda, no cuBLAS, and no ROCm, oneAPI or Metal in their place. The repository is aien-dev/CUDApp.
The qualified GPU today is the NVIDIA GB10 in the DGX Spark. On 2026-10-21 the 35 billion parameter model AIEN serves on the Spark was running on this code with zero CUDA libraries loaded.

The same program also runs in my own host code on Apple M and on x86_64, the CPU architecture AMD and Intel share, on branch feat/other-hardware. That path is not GPU machine code, and it is not a measured CUDA speed on those machines. AMD, Intel, and Apple GPUs are named and not qualified.
purpose_title: Less computation, out of the big data centers.
purpose: The goal is not a faster way to rent a data center. It is to need less of one: the same work with fewer bytes moved, fewer operations and fewer joules per answer, so it runs on a machine a person owns (a DGX Spark, a PC with one graphics card, a laptop). Every result is reported as work per answer, against the machine's own ceiling.
private_note: Public. The project name is CUDA++; its repository address is aien-dev/CUDApp. The licence and safety audit is docs/AUDIT.md, CLEAN for the history it covers.

hops.ours: The kernel builder, called from C. Omega's own languages reaching the GPU is Omega bar C1, built on this toolchain.
My own sm_121 encoder and register allocator: 59 instruction kinds, launch descriptors.
hops.note: every kernel the live server runs is encoded by it

hops.ours: My own client for the open kernel module's ioctls, written from its MIT headers.
Session, command lists and job engine: device, memory, upload, launch.
hops.note: one device, one process; no streams or events yet

hops.ours: Matrix multiply (BF16, FP8, 4 bit, ternary), decode and prefill attention, frozen-order reductions.
hops.note: shaped for the models AIEN runs; no any-shape GEMM yet

hops.ours: The motor, the ++ in CUDA++: one schedule built before anything runs, movement engines that check every weight part, and the stroke, many conversations on one read of the weights.
hops.note: historical 2026-10-21 serving receipt: 1.80x to 1.98x the same conversations taken in turn, not a CUDA comparison; branch result, not a current speed claim

hops.ours: AIEN's own GB10 driver. Its simulator gates pass; it has not run on the chip yet.
Stays NVIDIA's. The chip checks the firmware's signature and boots nothing else. CUDA++ never ships it.

how_lead: I built it alone on one DGX Spark in under four weeks, directing AI coding agents. NVIDIA publishes the source of its Linux kernel module, but not its compiler, its driver library or the GPU's machine code. So I skipped every closed layer.

steps.title: 1. The driver client, from the open kernel module's headers
steps.text: libcuda is closed, but everything it does to the hardware goes through ioctls that the open kernel module defines in its public headers. I copied 67 of those headers unchanged (MIT) and wrote my own client against them: client, device, address space, memory, command ring, compute object, doorbell, completion.

steps.title: 2. The machine code, reverse engineered
steps.text: NVIDIA does not publish the GPU's instruction encoding. I compiled small probe kernels of my own once with NVIDIA's compiler, read the machine code back with NVIDIA's disassembler as an offline oracle, and compared kernels that differ in one detail to see which bits mean what. I cross-checked against Mesa's open NVIDIA compiler, NAK, and believed nothing until the chip ran it and gave the right answer. The tensor-core arithmetic was measured on the chip over 2,048 cases until one model matched every output bit.

steps.title: 3. Launches in NVK's order
steps.text: A launch on Blackwell is a short list of commands in the channel ring. I took their order from Mesa's NVK Vulkan driver and the method offsets from the open headers, built my own command lists, and measured them: about 24 to 31 microseconds per extra dependent launch.

steps.title: 4. Built up, nothing counts until the chip agrees
steps.text: 2026-09-26 vector add on the GB10. 2026-10-02 numerics closed on the chip. 2026-10-13 my own probes measured the tensor cores at 115.14 TFLOPS and memory reads at 195.1 GB/s. 2026-10-21 a 35B model served on this code with zero CUDA libraries in the process.

did_not: I used no NVIDIA source code other than the open kernel module headers, and no NVIDIA binary. There is no libcuda, cubin, PTX or firmware in this repository or its history.
I did not take apart libcuda, nvcc or any other NVIDIA program. I ran NVIDIA's compiler and disassembler on my own small kernels and read what they printed.
I did not touch the GPU's firmware. It is still NVIDIA's, and the chip checks its signature.

I did not translate CUDA programs onto other chips. Other hardware runs my own code, and only where a receipt exists. Host execution has that receipt. GPU machine code on an AMD, Intel, or Apple GPU does not.
pain_lead: What makes CUDA hard to use and hard to leave, how CUDA++ fixes each one, and the command that shows it. A row is marked fixed only with its receipt.

pains.title: CUDA's pain points and the fix for each
pains.text: Written in docs/PAIN_POINTS.md on main: eleven pain points, each with a count, a source, and CUDA++'s answer. Some answers are done on the host (evidence/dx/); chip runs are still open, so this row stays in progress.

swap_lead: Take CUDA off a machine and put CUDA++ in its place, all the way down to the kernel driver, with one command each way.

swaps.title: User space: cudapp swap
swaps.text: The command is swap/cudapp on main: cudapp swap user and cudapp swap back, dry run unless --yes, every changed file copied first and checked by SHA-256 on the way back. A host test runs it on a fake root (tests/swap/test_swap_cli.sh). docs/SWAP.md is named in the script and is not on main, so this row stays in progress.

swaps.title: Kernel driver: cudapp swap kernel
swaps.text: The kernel level of the same command holds NVIDIA's modules back and loads AIEN's driver on the next boot. L401 is that command; L332 is the driver, whose simulator gates pass and which has not run on the chip yet.
